5. Linear and Nonlinear Approximation

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

When only a limited number of coefficients can be retained, the choice of representation determines which features of a signal survive. Approximation rates quantify this tradeoff and help explain the performance of compression and denoising methods. We compare fixed and adaptive coefficient selection, relate Fourier and wavelet errors to smoothness and edges, and examine triangulations and curvelets for images with smooth contours.

The analysis concerns functions f∈L2([0,1]d)f \in L^2([0,1]^d)f∈L2([0,1]d) on a continuous domain, with d=1,2d=1,2d=1,2.

5.1 Approximation¶

5.1.1 Approximation in an Orthonormal Basis¶

Let B={ψm}m\mathcal{B}= \{ \psi_m \}_mB={ψm​}m​ be an orthonormal basis of L2([0,1]d)L^2([0,1]^d)L2([0,1]d), with d=1d=1d=1 for signals or d=2d=2d=2 for images. The complete expansion in this basis,

f=∑m∈Z⟨f, ψm⟩ψmf = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} \langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle \psi_mf=m∈Z∑​⟨f,ψm​⟩ψm​

reconstructs the signal exactly. Approximation and processing methods modify the coefficients ⟨f, ψm⟩\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle⟨f,ψm​⟩, introducing a reconstruction error.

The simplest approximation reconstructs the signal from a subset IM⊂ZI_M \subset \mathbb{Z}IM​⊂Z of MMM coefficients:

fM:=∑m∈IM⟨f, ψm⟩ψm,whereM=∣IM∣.f_M \mathrel{:=}\sum_{m \in I_M} \langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle \psi_m, \quad \text{where} \quad M = |I_M|.fM​:=m∈IM​∑​⟨f,ψm​⟩ψm​,whereM=∣IM​∣.

The reconstructed signal fMf_MfM​ is the orthogonal projection of fff onto the space

VM:=Span{ψm  ;  m∈IM}.V_M \mathrel{:=}\mathop{\mathrm{Span}} \left\{ \psi_m \;;\; m \in I_M \right\} .VM​:=Span{ψm​;m∈IM​}.

If the selected space VMV_MVM​ depends on fff, the overall approximation map f↦fMf \mapsto f_Mf↦fM​ may be nonlinear, even though projection onto each fixed space is linear.

Since the basis is orthogonal, the approximation error is

∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣2=∑m∉IM∣⟨f, ψm⟩∣2.|\!| f-f_M |\!|^2 = \sum_{m \notin I_M} |\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle|^2.∣∣f−fM​∣∣2=m∈/IM​∑​∣⟨f,ψm​⟩∣2.

The central choice is the retained index set IMI_MIM​, which may depend on the signal fff.

5.1.2 Linear Approximation¶

Fixing IMI_MIM​ independently of the input gives a linear approximation: the same coefficients are retained for every fff. The map f↦fMf \mapsto f_Mf↦fM​ is then orthogonal projection onto a fixed space VMV_MVM​, and it satisfies

(f+g)M=fM+gM(f+g)_M = f_M + g_M(f+g)M​=fM​+gM​

For the Fourier basis and an even coefficient budget, one usually selects the low-frequency atoms

IM={−M/2+1,…,M/2}.I_M = \{-M/2+1,\ldots,M/2\}.IM​={−M/2+1,…,M/2}.

For a 1-D wavelet basis, one usually selects the coarse wavelets

IM={coarsest scaling atoms and wavelets (j,n) with j⩾j0}I_M=\{\text{coarsest scaling atoms and wavelets }(j,n)\text{ with }j\geqslant j_0\}IM​={coarsest scaling atoms and wavelets (j,n) with j⩾j0​}

where j0j_0j0​ is selected such that ∣IM∣=M|I_M|=M∣IM​∣=M.

Figure 5.1. Linear versus nonlinear wavelet approximation.

Figure 5.1, center, illustrates linear wavelet approximation. Discarding all fine-scale details blurs singularities, where the approximation is least accurate.

5.1.3 Nonlinear Approximation¶

Allowing IMI_MIM​ to depend on fff gives a nonlinear approximation. To choose IMI_MIM​ that minimizes ∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣|\!| f-f_M |\!|∣∣f−fM​∣∣, orthogonality reduces the problem to retaining the MMM coefficients of largest magnitude:

IM={M largest coefficients ∣⟨f, ψm⟩∣}.I_M= \{ M \text{ largest coefficients } |\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle| \}.IM​={M largest coefficients ∣⟨f,ψm​⟩∣}.

When there are no ties at the cutoff, this can be obtained by thresholding

IM={m  ;  ∣⟨f, ψm⟩∣>T}I_M = \left\{ m \;;\; |\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle|>T \right\}IM​={m;∣⟨f,ψm​⟩∣>T}

where TTT depends on the number of coefficients MMM,

M=#{m  ;  ∣⟨f, ψm⟩∣>T}.M = \# \left\{ m \;;\; |\langle f,\,\psi_m\rangle|>T \right\} .M=#{m;∣⟨f,ψm​⟩∣>T}.

5.2 Signal and Image Modeling¶

A signal model specifies a constraint f∈Θf \in \Thetaf∈Θ, where Θ⊂L2([0,1]d)\Theta \subset L^2([0,1]^d)Θ⊂L2([0,1]d) is the class of signals of interest. Figure 5.4 shows different image models, which we describe below.

5.2.1 Uniformly Smooth Signals and Images¶

Signals with derivatives.

The simplest model consists of uniformly smooth signals with bounded derivatives

Θ={f∈L2([0,1]d)  ;  ∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Cα⩽C},(5.5)\Theta= \left\{ f \in L^2([0,1]^d) \;;\; |\!| f |\!|_{\text{C}^\alpha} \leqslant C \right\} , \tag{5.5}Θ={f∈L2([0,1]d);∣∣f∣∣Cα​⩽C},(5.5)

where C>0C>0C>0 is fixed. For integer α⩾1\alpha\geqslant 1α⩾1, in one dimension

∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Cα:=max⁡0⩽k⩽α  ∣ ⁣∣dkfdtk∣ ⁣∣∞.|\!| f |\!|_{\text{C}^\alpha} \mathrel{:=}\underset{0\leqslant k\leqslant\alpha}{\max}\; \Big|\!\Big| \frac{\mathrm{d}^k f}{\mathrm{d}t^k} \Big |\!\Big|_{\infty}.∣∣f∣∣Cα​:=0⩽k⩽αmax​∣∣​∣∣​dtkdkf​∣∣​∣∣​∞​.

In higher dimensions, take the maximum over all partial derivatives of total order at most α\alphaα. For noninteger α=m+β\alpha=m+\betaα=m+β, 0<β<10<\beta<10<β<1, use the usual Hölder norm: derivatives through order mmm are bounded, and order-mmm derivatives are β\betaβ-Hölder continuous.

Sobolev smooth signals and images.

For integer α⩾1\alpha\geqslant 1α⩾1, a Cα\text{C}^\alphaCα signal in the model (5.5) has derivatives with bounded energy:

dαfdtα(t)=f(α)(t)∈L2([0,1]).\frac{\mathrm{d}^\alpha f}{\mathrm{d}t^\alpha}(t) = f^{(\alpha)}(t) \in L^2([0,1]).dtαdαf​(t)=f(α)(t)∈L2([0,1]).

For integer α\alphaα and periodic boundary conditions, use the identity

f^m(α)=(2iπm)αf^m\hat f^{(\alpha)}_m = (2i\pi m)^\alpha\hat f_mf^​m(α)​=(2iπm)αf^​m​

Here f^\hat ff^​ denotes Fourier coefficients as in (2.2), now on R/Z\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}R/Z rather than R/2πZ\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}R/2πZ:

f^n:=∫01e−2iπnxf(x)dx,\hat f_n \mathrel{:=}\int_0^1 e^{-2\mathrm{i}\pi n x} f(x) \mathrm{d}x,f^​n​:=∫01​e−2iπnxf(x)dx,

This motivates the homogeneous Sobolev seminorm

∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Sob(α)2=∑m∈Z∣2πm∣2α∣⟨f, em⟩∣2,(5.6)|\!| f |\!|_{\text{Sob}(\alpha)}^2 = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} |2\pi m|^{2\alpha} |\langle f,\,e_m\rangle|^2, \tag{5.6}∣∣f∣∣Sob(α)2​=m∈Z∑​∣2πm∣2α∣⟨f,em​⟩∣2,(5.6)

so that ∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Sob(α)=∣ ⁣∣f(α)∣ ⁣∣|\!| f |\!|_{\text{Sob}(\alpha)} = |\!| f^{(\alpha)} |\!|∣∣f∣∣Sob(α)​=∣∣f(α)∣∣ for smooth periodic functions. The same seminorm applies when the derivatives exist only in the distributional sense and belong to L2([0,1])L^2([0,1])L2([0,1]).

This definition extends to distributions and signals f∈L2([0,1]d)f \in L^2([0,1]^d)f∈L2([0,1]d) of arbitrary dimension ddd as

The periodic Sobolev model

Θ={f∈L2([0,1]d)  ;  ∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣22+∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Sob(α)2⩽C}(5.8)\Theta= \left\{ f \in L^2([0,1]^d) \;;\; |\!| f |\!|_2^2+|\!| f |\!|_{\text{Sob}(\alpha)}^2\leqslant C \right\} \tag{5.8}Θ={f∈L2([0,1]d);∣∣f∣∣22​+∣∣f∣∣Sob(α)2​⩽C}(5.8)

5.2.2 Piecewise Regular Signals and Images¶

Piecewise smooth signals.

A piecewise smooth 1-D signal f∈L2([0,1])f \in L^2([0,1])f∈L2([0,1]) is Cα\text{C}^\alphaCα on the intervals separated by at most KKK interior singular points:

Θ={f∈L2([0,1])  ;  ∃ 0=t0<t1<⋯<tK+1=1,max⁡0⩽i⩽K∣ ⁣∣f∣(ti,ti+1)∣ ⁣∣Cα⩽C}(5.9)\Theta= \left\{ f \in L^2([0,1]) \;;\; \exists\,0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_{K+1}=1,\quad\max_{0\leqslant i\leqslant K}|\!| f|_{(t_i,t_{i+1})} |\!|_{\text{C}^\alpha}\leqslant C \right\} \tag{5.9}Θ={f∈L2([0,1]);∃0=t0​<t1​<⋯<tK+1​=1,0⩽i⩽Kmax​∣∣f∣(ti​,ti+1​)​∣∣Cα​⩽C}(5.9)

Here f∣(ti,ti+1)f|_{(t_i,t_{i+1})}f∣(ti​,ti+1​)​ denotes the restriction of fff to the open interval (ti,ti+1)(t_i,t_{i+1})(ti​,ti+1​).

Piecewise smooth images.

A piecewise smooth image is a function f∈L2([0,1]2)f \in L^2([0,1]^2)f∈L2([0,1]2) with Cα\text{C}^\alphaCα regularity away from at most KKK rectifiable curves:

Θ={f∈L2([0,1]2)  ;  ∃ Γ=⋃i=0K−1γi,  ∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Cα(Γc)⩽C1and∣γi∣⩽C2}(5.10)\Theta= \left\{ f \in L^2([0,1]^2) \;;\; \exists \, \Gamma=\bigcup_{i=0}^{K-1}\gamma_i, \; |\!| f |\!|_{\text{C}^\alpha(\Gamma^c)} \leqslant C_1 \quad \text{and} \quad |\gamma_i| \leqslant C_2 \right\} \tag{5.10}Θ={f∈L2([0,1]2);∃Γ=i=0⋃K−1​γi​,∣∣f∣∣Cα(Γc)​⩽C1​and∣γi​∣⩽C2​}(5.10)

Here ∣γi∣|\gamma_i|∣γi​∣ denotes curve length. The CαC^\alphaCα bound applies separately within each smooth region, with uniform one-sided regularity up to its edges.

Segmentation methods such as the one proposed by Mumford and Shah [24] implicitly assume such a piecewise smooth image model.

5.2.3 Bounded Variation Signals and Images¶

Bounded variation provides a more flexible model for signals with edges

Θ={f∈L2([0,1]d)  ;  ∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣∞⩽C1and∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣TV⩽C2}.(5.11)\Theta= \left\{ f\in L^2([0,1]^d) \;;\; |\!| f |\!|_{\infty} \leqslant C_1 \quad \text{and} \quad |\!| f |\!|_{\text{TV}} \leqslant C_2 \right\} . \tag{5.11}Θ={f∈L2([0,1]d);∣∣f∣∣∞​⩽C1​and∣∣f∣∣TV​⩽C2​}.(5.11)

For d=1d=1d=1 and d=2d=2d=2, this model includes the piecewise smooth signal and image models (5.9) and (5.10) when α⩾1\alpha\geqslant 1α⩾1, after adjusting the constants. Bounds on the derivatives, jump sizes, and total edge length then control the variation.

The total variation of a smooth function is

∫∣ ⁣∣∇f(x)∣ ⁣∣dx\int |\!| \nabla f(x) |\!| \mathrm{d}x∫∣∣∇f(x)∣∣dx

where

∇f(x)=(∂f∂xi)i=0d−1∈Rd\nabla f(x) = \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} \right)_{i=0}^{d-1} \in \mathbb{R}^d∇f(x)=(∂xi​∂f​)i=0d−1​∈Rd

is the gradient at xxx. Total variation also extends to discontinuous images, including those with jumps across edges. The coarea formula expresses the total variation of a piecewise smooth image as an integral of the perimeters of its superlevel sets:

∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣TV=∫−∞∞Per⁡({f>t};Ω) dt,Ω=(0,1)d.(5.12)|\!| f |\!|_{\text{TV}}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{Per}(\{f>t\};\Omega)\,\mathrm{d}t,\qquad\Omega=(0,1)^d. \tag{5.12}∣∣f∣∣TV​=∫−∞∞​Per({f>t};Ω)dt,Ω=(0,1)d.(5.12)

Here the perimeter is relative to the image domain. For smooth functions in two dimensions it agrees, for almost every ttt, with the length of the level curve. For a bounded set Ω⊂R2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^2Ω⊂R2 with piecewise smooth boundary, taking total variation on all of R2\mathbb{R}^2R2 gives

∣ ⁣∣1Ω∣ ⁣∣TV=∣∂Ω∣.|\!| 1_\Omega |\!|_{\text{TV}} = |\partial \Omega|.∣∣1Ω​∣∣TV​=∣∂Ω∣.

The model of bounded variation was introduced in image processing by Rudin, Osher and Fatemi [28].

5.2.4 Cartoon Images¶

The bounded-variation model (5.11) controls total perimeter but does not require individual edges to be smooth. For images with smooth contours, incorporating that additional geometry can improve approximation and processing.

The Cα\text{C}^\alphaCα cartoon model consists of 2-D functions that are Cα\text{C}^\alphaCα away from at most KKK smooth edge curves γi\gamma_iγi​:

Θ={f∈L2([0,1]2)  ;  ∃ Γ=⋃i=0K−1γi,  ∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Cα(Γc)⩽C1and∣ ⁣∣γi∣ ⁣∣Cα⩽C2}(5.13)\Theta= \left\{ f \in L^2([0,1]^2) \;;\; \exists \, \Gamma=\bigcup_{i=0}^{K-1}\gamma_i, \; |\!| f |\!|_{\text{C}^\alpha(\Gamma^c)} \leqslant C_1 \quad \text{and} \quad |\!| \gamma_i |\!|_{\text{C}^\alpha} \leqslant C_2 \right\} \tag{5.13}Θ={f∈L2([0,1]2);∃Γ=i=0⋃K−1​γi​,∣∣f∣∣Cα(Γc)​⩽C1​and∣∣γi​∣∣Cα​⩽C2​}(5.13)

Each curve is parameterized by arc length on [0,Ai][0,A_i][0,Ai​], with a uniform bound on AiA_iAi​ and its CαC^\alphaCα norm. Figure 5.6 illustrates a progressive dead-leaves construction: opaque shapes are placed successively, producing smooth visible contour segments and occlusion boundaries.

Figure 5.6. Progressive dead-leaves construction: later opaque shapes cover earlier ones, producing a family of cartoon images.

Optical diffraction can blur these edges, motivating the blurred cartoon model

Θ~={f~=f⋆h∈L2([0,1]2)  ;  f∈Θandh∈H}(5.14)\tilde\Theta= \left\{ \tilde f = f \star h \in L^2([0,1]^2) \;;\; f \in \Theta \quad \text{and} \quad h \in \mathcal{H} \right\} \tag{5.14}Θ~={f~​=f⋆h∈L2([0,1]2);f∈Θandh∈H}(5.14)

where Θ\ThetaΘ is the sharp-image model (5.13) and H\mathcal{H}H specifies the admissible blur kernels. For example, h⩾0h \geqslant 0h⩾0 may be required to be smooth and localized in both space and frequency. Unknown blur makes it difficult to first detect the edges Γ\GammaΓ and then process the smooth regions separately.

5.3 Efficient Approximation¶

5.3.1 Decay of Approximation Error¶

To process signals in Θ\ThetaΘ efficiently, we seek an orthonormal basis in which the nonlinear approximation error ∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣|\!| f-f_M |\!|∣∣f−fM​∣∣ tends to 0 as rapidly as possible when MMM grows.

Polynomial error decay.

This error decay is measured using a power law

∀ f∈Θ,  ∀ M,∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣2⩽CfM−α(5.15)\forall \,f \in \Theta, \; \forall \,M, \quad |\!| f-f_M |\!|^2 \leqslant C_f M^{-\alpha} \tag{5.15}∀f∈Θ,∀M,∣∣f−fM​∣∣2⩽Cf​M−α(5.15)

Here α\alphaα is common to all signals in the model; larger values mean faster decay. The exponent depends on the basis and the model Θ\ThetaΘ, and measures how efficiently the basis represents that class. The constant CfC_fCf​ may depend on the particular signal fff.

Relevance for compression, denoising and inverse problems.

Approximation rates have practical consequences. Section 6.1 relates compression error to nonlinear approximation error, explaining why an effective approximation basis also supports efficient compression.

Chapter 7 develops a similar connection for thresholding denoisers. Thresholding forms a nonlinear approximation of the noisy image, and the expected denoising error is controlled by how well the basis approximates the clean signal.

Chapter 10 uses compressibility in a chosen basis to address inverse problems such as super-resolution and inpainting. Efficient approximation of the unknown signal helps recover missing information, provided the measurement operator retains enough information about sparse combinations of basis atoms. Recovery performance therefore depends on both the basis and the measurements.

Comparison of signals.

With the basis fixed, the decay of ∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣|\!| f-f_M |\!|∣∣f−fM​∣∣ compares the approximation complexity of different images. Figure 5.9 illustrates how intricate geometry and textures slow down wavelet approximation.

To reveal approximate power-law behavior, the error curves are displayed on logarithmic axes. An exact power law has the form

log⁡(∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣2)=cst−αlog⁡(M)\log(|\!| f-f_M |\!|^2) = \text{cst} - \alpha\log(M)log(∣∣f−fM​∣∣2)=cst−αlog(M)

and appears as a straight line with slope −α-\alpha−α. For sampled data, this behavior is generally studied when M≪NM \ll NM≪N; as M≈NM \approx NM≈N, retaining nearly all coefficients drives the error to zero.

Figure 5.8. Test images with different structures: smooth, cartoon, flower, and mandrill.

Figure 5.9. Wavelet approximation error for the images in Figure 5.8.

5.3.2 Comparison of bases.¶

For a fixed image fff, the decay of ∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣|\!| f-f_M |\!|∣∣f−fM​∣∣ compares the efficiency of different bases. Figure 5.11 makes this comparison for an image containing contours and textures. The Fourier basis of Section 2.5 performs poorly here: periodic boundaries create artifacts, and globally supported atoms do not follow local contours. The cosine basis removes the periodic boundary discontinuity through symmetric extension, but its atoms remain global. Local DCT bases use cosine atoms on small square patches, improving localization. At small coefficient budgets MMM, however, their block structure produces visible artifacts. The isotropic wavelet basis of Section 4.5.2 performs best in this example by combining localized atoms with a multiresolution organization.

Figure 5.11. Comparison of approximation error decay for different bases.

5.4 Fourier Linear Approximation of Smooth Functions¶

For integer α\alphaα, the smooth model (5.5) bounds all continuous derivatives through that order. Greater regularity of fff, measured by a larger α\alphaα, permits faster approximation. Figure 5.5 illustrates the related Sobolev measure of smoothness.

5.4.1 1-D Fourier Approximation¶

A 1-D signal f∈L2([0,1])f \in L^2([0,1])f∈L2([0,1]) is associated with a 1-periodic function f(t+1)=f(t)f(t+1)=f(t)f(t+1)=f(t) defined for t∈Rt \in \mathbb{R}t∈R.

Low pass approximation.

For even MMM, consider the linear Fourier approximation that retains frequencies up to M/2M/2M/2:

fMlin=∑m=−M/2M/2⟨f, em⟩emf_M^{\text{lin}} = \sum_{m=-M/2}^{M/2} \langle f,\,e_m\rangle e_mfMlin​=m=−M/2∑M/2​⟨f,em​⟩em​

where we use the 1-D Fourier atoms

∀ m∈Z,em(t):=e2iπmt.\forall \,m\in\mathbb{Z},\quad e_m(t) \mathrel{:=}e^{2 i \pi m t}.∀m∈Z,em​(t):=e2iπmt.

This symmetric cutoff retains M+1M+1M+1 Fourier atoms; the extra coefficient does not affect the asymptotic rates below.

Figure 5.13 shows these approximations for increasing MMM. The jumps in fff produce substantial error and ringing near the singularities.

Figure 5.13. Fourier approximation of a signal.

This low-pass approximation is a convolution, since

fM=∑m=−M/2M/2⟨f, em⟩em=f⋆hMwhereh^M:=1[−M/2,M/2].f_M = \sum_{m=-M/2}^{M/2} \langle f,\,e_m\rangle e_m = f \star h_M \quad \text{where} \quad \hat h_{M} \mathrel{:=}1_{[-M/2,M/2]}.fM​=m=−M/2∑M/2​⟨f,em​⟩em​=f⋆hM​whereh^M​:=1[−M/2,M/2]​.

The kernel hMh_MhM​ is the Dirichlet kernel introduced in the Fourier chapter.

The following elementary bound shows that this approximation error decays for Cα\mathcal{C}^\alphaCα signals.

Proposition 5.2

For integer α⩾1\alpha\geqslant 1α⩾1 and f∈Cα(R/Z)f\in C^\alpha(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})f∈Cα(R/Z)

∣ ⁣∣f−fMlin∣ ⁣∣2=O(M−2α+1).|\!| f-f_M^{\text{lin}} |\!|^2 = O(M^{-2\alpha+1}).∣∣f−fMlin​∣∣2=O(M−2α+1).

Using integration by parts, one shows that for a Cα\text{C}^\alphaCα function fff in the smooth signal model (5.5), F(f(ℓ))m=(2imπ)ℓf^m\mathcal{F}(f^{(\ell)})_m = (2\mathrm{i}m \pi)^\ell \hat f_mF(f(ℓ))m​=(2imπ)ℓf^​m​, so that Cauchy–Schwarz gives

∣⟨f, em⟩∣⩽∣2πm∣−α∣ ⁣∣f(α)∣ ⁣∣2.|\langle f,\,e_m\rangle| \leqslant|2\pi m|^{-\alpha} |\!| f^{(\alpha)} |\!|_2.∣⟨f,em​⟩∣⩽∣2πm∣−α∣∣f(α)∣∣2​.

This implies

∣ ⁣∣f−fMlin∣ ⁣∣2=∑∣m∣>M/2∣⟨f, em⟩∣2⩽∣ ⁣∣f(α)∣ ⁣∣22∑∣m∣>M/2∣2πm∣−2α=O(M−2α+1).|\!| f-f_M^{\text{lin}} |\!|^2 = \sum_{|m|>M/2} |\langle f,\,e_m\rangle|^2 \leqslant|\!| f^{(\alpha)} |\!|^2_2 \sum_{|m|>M/2} |2\pi m|^{-2\alpha} = O(M^{-2\alpha+1}).∣∣f−fMlin​∣∣2=∣m∣>M/2∑​∣⟨f,em​⟩∣2⩽∣∣f(α)∣∣22​∣m∣>M/2∑​∣2πm∣−2α=O(M−2α+1).

Using the full energy of f(α)f^{(\alpha)}f(α) gives a sharper bound under the same assumptions. The argument also applies to the larger Sobolev class.

Proposition 5.3

For α>0\alpha>0α>0 and a periodic signal in the Sobolev model (5.8), one has

∣ ⁣∣f−fMlin∣ ⁣∣2⩽C∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Sob(α)2M−2α.(5.16)|\!| f-f^{\text{lin}}_M |\!|^2 \leqslant C |\!| f |\!|_{\mathrm{Sob}(\alpha)}^2 M^{-2\alpha}. \tag{5.16}∣∣f−fMlin​∣∣2⩽C∣∣f∣∣Sob(α)2​M−2α.(5.16)
Proof

One has

∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Sob(α)2=∑m∣2πm∣2α∣⟨f, em⟩∣2⩾∑∣m∣>M/2∣2πm∣2α∣⟨f, em⟩∣2(5.17)\begin{aligned} |\!| f |\!|_{\mathrm{Sob}(\alpha)}^2 &= \sum_m |2 \pi m|^{2\alpha} |\langle f,\,e_m\rangle|^2 \geqslant\sum_{|m|>M/2} |2 \pi m|^{2\alpha} |\langle f,\,e_m\rangle|^2 \end{aligned} \tag{5.17}∣∣f∣∣Sob(α)2​​=m∑​∣2πm∣2α∣⟨f,em​⟩∣2⩾∣m∣>M/2∑​∣2πm∣2α∣⟨f,em​⟩∣2​(5.17)

This rate is optimal uniformly over a Sobolev ball. The best MMM-term Fourier approximation satisfies the same upper bound because it is at least as accurate as the low-pass approximation; individual functions may have faster decay.

and Fourier atoms are no longer optimal for approximation.

For example, the interval indicator f=1[a,b]f=1_{[a,b]}f=1[a,b]​ has coefficients f^m=(e−2πima−e−2πimb)/(2πim)\hat f_m=(e^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}ma}-e^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}mb})/(2\pi\mathrm{i}m)f^​m​=(e−2πima−e−2πimb)/(2πim) for m≠0m\neq0m=0, and hence ∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣2≍M−1|\!| f-f_M |\!|^2\asymp M^{-1}∣∣f−fM​∣∣2≍M−1 when 0<b−a<10<b-a<10<b−a<1 for both linear and nonlinear approximations.

5.4.2 Sobolev Images¶

The same argument applies to images and higher-dimensional data through the Sobolev seminorm (5.7) with d>1d>1d>1.

For an α\alphaα-regular Sobolev image, the linear and nonlinear approximation errors satisfy

∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣2⩽C∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣Sob(α)2M−α.|\!| f-f_M |\!|^2 \leqslant C |\!| f |\!|_{\mathrm{Sob}(\alpha)}^2 M^{-\alpha}.∣∣f−fM​∣∣2⩽C∣∣f∣∣Sob(α)2​M−α.

For ddd-dimensional data f:[0,1]d→Rf : [0,1]^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}f:[0,1]d→R, the corresponding error bound is O(M−2α/d)O(M^{-2\alpha/d})O(M−2α/d).

For an image with piecewise Lipschitz regularity and finite-length edges in the model (5.10), the linear and nonlinear errors satisfy the slower general bound

∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣2⩽CfM−1/2,(5.20)|\!| f-f_M |\!|^2 \leqslant C_f M^{-1/2}, \tag{5.20}∣∣f−fM​∣∣2⩽Cf​M−1/2,(5.20)

and Fourier atoms are no longer optimal for approximation.

5.5 Wavelet Approximation of Piecewise Smooth Functions¶

Wavelets improve approximation near singularities because their support is localized.

5.5.1 Decay of Wavelet Coefficients¶

To approximate smooth regions efficiently, choose wavelets with sufficiently many vanishing moments, denoted by ppp:

∀ k=0,…,p−1,  ∫ψ(x)xkdx=0.\forall \,k=0,\ldots,p-1, \; \int \psi(x) x^k \mathrm{d}x = 0.∀k=0,…,p−1,∫ψ(x)xkdx=0.

Choose p⩾αp\geqslant\alphap⩾α, where α\alphaα is the regularity of the signal outside singularities (for instance jumps or kinks).

Figure 5.15. Singular and regular regions of a signal (left) and an image (right).

To quantify the approximation error decay for piecewise smooth signals (5.9) and images (5.10), one treats wavelets supported in smooth regions separately from those crossing singularities. Figure 5.15 locates the singular and regular regions of a signal and an image.

Proposition 5.4

Assume a compactly supported wavelet with p⩾αp\geqslant\alphap⩾α vanishing moments (all moments of total degree less than ppp in dimension ddd). If fff admits a CαC^\alphaCα extension to a neighborhood of the support, one has

∣⟨f, ψj,n⟩∣⩽Cf2j(α+d/2)∫∣t∣α∣ψ(t)∣ dt.(5.21)|\langle f,\,\psi_{j,n}\rangle| \leqslant C_f2^{j(\alpha+d/2)}\int|t|^\alpha|\psi(t)|\,\mathrm{d}t. \tag{5.21}∣⟨f,ψj,n​⟩∣⩽Cf​2j(α+d/2)∫∣t∣α∣ψ(t)∣dt.(5.21)

Without the smoothness assumption, every bounded fff satisfies

∣⟨f, ψj,n⟩∣⩽∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣∞∣ ⁣∣ψ∣ ⁣∣12jd2.(5.22)|\langle f,\,\psi_{j,n}\rangle| \leqslant|\!| f |\!|_\infty |\!| \psi |\!|_1 2^{j \frac{d}{2}}. \tag{5.22}∣⟨f,ψj,n​⟩∣⩽∣∣f∣∣∞​∣∣ψ∣∣1​2j2d​.(5.22)
Proof

Under these assumptions, one can perform a Taylor expansion of fff around the point 2jn2^j n2jn

f(x)=P(x−2jn)+R(x−2jn)=P(2jt)+R(2jt)f(x) = P(x-2^j n) + R(x-2^jn) = P(2^j t) + R(2^j t)f(x)=P(x−2jn)+R(x−2jn)=P(2jt)+R(2jt)

where deg⁡(P)<α\deg(P)<\alphadeg(P)<α and

∣R(x)∣⩽Cf∣ ⁣∣x∣ ⁣∣α.|R(x)|\leqslant C_f |\!| x |\!|^\alpha.∣R(x)∣⩽Cf​∣∣x∣∣α.

One then bounds the wavelet coefficient

⟨f, ψj,n⟩=12jd2∫f(x)ψ(x−2jn2j)dx=2jd2∫R(2jt)ψ(t)dt\langle f,\,\psi_{j,n}\rangle = \frac{1}{2^{j \frac{d}{2}}} \int f(x) \psi\left( \frac{x-2^j n}{2^j} \right) \mathrm{d}x = 2^{j \frac{d}{2}} \int R(2^j t) \psi(t) \mathrm{d}t⟨f,ψj,n​⟩=2j2d​1​∫f(x)ψ(2jx−2jn​)dx=2j2d​∫R(2jt)ψ(t)dt

where we substituted t=x−2jn2jt = \frac{x-2^j n}{2^j}t=2jx−2jn​. This proves (5.21). The bound (5.22) follows directly by bounding the function in the inner product.

5.5.2 1-D Piecewise Smooth Approximation¶

For a piecewise smooth 1-D signal in the model (5.9), the large coefficients ⟨f, ψj,n⟩\langle f,\,\psi_{j,n}\rangle⟨f,ψj,n​⟩ concentrate near singularities. Denote the finite set of singular points by S⊂[0,1]\mathcal{S}\subset [0,1]S⊂[0,1].

For α>0\alpha>0α>0, let fff belong to the piecewise CαC^\alphaCα model (5.9). With compactly supported orthonormal wavelets having at least α\alphaα vanishing moments (and a compatible boundary construction), the best MMM-term error satisfies

∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣2=O(M−2α).(5.23)|\!| f-f_M |\!|^2 = O(M^{-2\alpha}). \tag{5.23}∣∣f−fM​∣∣2=O(M−2α).(5.23)
Proof

The proof is split into several parts.

Step 1. Separating regular and singular coefficients.

At scale 2j2^j2j, define the singular index set by the wavelets whose support crosses a singularity:

Cj={n  ;  supp(ψj,n)∩S≠∅}(5.24)\mathcal{C}_j = \left\{ n \;;\; \mathop{\mathrm{supp}}(\psi_{j,n}) \cap \mathcal{S}\neq \emptyset \right\} \tag{5.24}Cj​={n;supp(ψj,n​)∩S=∅}(5.24)

∣Cj∣⩽K∣S∣=constant.|\mathcal{C}_j| \leqslant K |\mathcal{S}| = \text{constant}.∣Cj​∣⩽K∣S∣=constant.

Using (5.21) for d=1d=1d=1, the decay of regular coefficients is bounded as

∀ n∈Cjc,∣⟨f, ψj,n⟩∣⩽C2j(α+1/2).\forall \,n \in \mathcal{C}_j^c, \quad \left\lvert\langle f,\,\psi_{j,n}\rangle\right\rvert \leqslant C2^{j(\alpha+1/2)}.∀n∈Cjc​,∣⟨f,ψj,n​⟩∣⩽C2j(α+1/2).

Using (5.22) for d=1d=1d=1, the decay of singular coefficients is bounded as

∀ n∈Cj,∣⟨f, ψj,n⟩∣⩽C2j/2.\forall \,n \in \mathcal{C}_j, \quad \left\lvert\langle f,\,\psi_{j,n}\rangle\right\rvert \leqslant C 2^{j/2}.∀n∈Cj​,∣⟨f,ψj,n​⟩∣⩽C2j/2.

For a sufficiently small threshold TTT, define two cutoff scales, one for regular coefficients and one for singular coefficients, as functions of TTT:

2j1=(T/C)1α+1/2and2j2=(T/C)2.2^{j_1} = (T/C)^{\frac{1}{\alpha+1/2}} \quad \text{and} \quad 2^{j_2} = (T/C)^{2}.2j1​=(T/C)α+1/21​and2j2​=(T/C)2.

Round these cutoff scales to integers; this changes constants only. All subsequent scale sums are bounded above by the fixed coarsest scale j0=0j_0=0j0​=0, and the finitely many scaling coefficients are retained. ⩽∑j<j2(K∣S∣)×C22j+∑j<j12−j×C22j(2α+1)(5.27)\begin{aligned} & \leqslant\sum_{j < j_2} (K |\mathcal{S}|) \times C^2 2^{j} + \sum_{j < j_1} 2^{-j} \times C^2 2^{j(2\alpha+1)} \end{aligned} \tag{5.27}​⩽j<j2​∑​(K∣S∣)×C22j+j<j1​∑​2−j×C22j(2α+1)​(5.27)
=O(2j2+22αj1)=O(T2+T2αα+1/2)=O(T2αα+1/2).(5.28)\begin{aligned} & = O( 2^{j_2} + 2^{2\alpha j_1} ) = O( T^2 + T^{ \frac{2\alpha}{\alpha+1/2} } ) = O( T^{ \frac{2\alpha}{\alpha+1/2} } ). \end{aligned} \tag{5.28}​=O(2j2​+22αj1​)=O(T2+Tα+1/22α​)=O(Tα+1/22α​).​(5.28)

=O(∣log⁡(T)∣+T−1α+1/2)=O(T−1α+1/2).(5.30)\begin{aligned} &= O( |\log(T)| + T^{\frac{-1}{\alpha+1/2}} ) = O(T^{\frac{-1}{\alpha+1/2}} ). \end{aligned} \tag{5.30}​=O(∣log(T)∣+Tα+1/2−1​)=O(Tα+1/2−1​).​(5.30)

Step 4. Putting everything together.

Given a coefficient budget MMM, choose TTT to be a sufficiently large constant times M−(α+1/2)M^{-(\alpha+1/2)}M−(α+1/2). The coefficient-count bound then uses at most MMM terms, and the error bound is O(M−2α)O(M^{-2\alpha})O(M−2α).

5.5.3 2-D Piecewise Smooth Approximation¶

We now give the counterpart of Theorem 5.5 for 2-D functions.

Theorem 5.6

Let fff belong to the piecewise smooth image model (5.10), with α⩾1\alpha\geqslant 1α⩾1 and finitely many rectifiable edge curves. For compactly supported orthonormal wavelets with at least α\alphaα vanishing moments and compatible boundary treatment, the best MMM-term error satisfies

∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣2=O(M−1).(5.31)|\!| f-f_M |\!|^2 = O(M^{-1}). \tag{5.31}∣∣f−fM​∣∣2=O(M−1).(5.31)

For an image in the model (5.10), define the singular index set Cj\mathcal{C}_jCj​ as in (5.24). Unlike the 1-D case, its cardinality grows as the scale 2j2^j2j decreases:

∣Cjω∣⩽2−jK∣S∣,|\mathcal{C}_j^\omega| \leqslant 2^{-j} K |\mathcal{S}|,∣Cjω​∣⩽2−jK∣S∣,

where ∣S∣|\mathcal{S}|∣S∣ is the total length of the singular curves S\mathcal{S}S, and ω∈{V,H,D}\omega\in \{V,H,D\}ω∈{V,H,D} is the wavelet orientation. Using (5.21) for d=2d=2d=2, the decay of regular coefficients is bounded as

∀ n∈(Cjω)c,∣⟨f, ψj,nω⟩∣⩽C2j(α+1).\forall \,n \in (\mathcal{C}_j^{\omega})^c, \quad \left\lvert\langle f,\,\psi_{j,n}^\omega\rangle\right\rvert \leqslant C2^{j(\alpha+1)}.∀n∈(Cjω​)c,∣∣​⟨f,ψj,nω​⟩∣∣​⩽C2j(α+1).

Using (5.22) for d=2d=2d=2, the decay of singular coefficients is bounded as

∀ n∈Cjω,∣⟨f, ψj,nω⟩∣⩽C2j.\forall \,n \in \mathcal{C}_j^\omega, \quad \left\lvert\langle f,\,\psi_{j,n}^\omega\rangle\right\rvert \leqslant C 2^{j}.∀n∈Cjω​,∣∣​⟨f,ψj,nω​⟩∣∣​⩽C2j.

After fixing TTT, the cut-off scales are defined as

2j1=(T/C)1α+1and2j2=T/C.2^{j_1} = (T/C)^{\frac{1}{\alpha+1}} \quad \text{and} \quad 2^{j_2} = T/C.2j1​=(T/C)α+11​and2j2​=T/C.

We define, as in (5.25), a comparison approximation. Similarly to (5.26), we bound the approximation error as

∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣2⩽∣ ⁣∣f−f~M∣ ⁣∣2=O(2j2+22αj1)=O(T+T2αα+1)=O(T)|\!| f-f_M |\!|^2 \leqslant|\!| f-\tilde f_M |\!|^2 = O( 2^{j_2} + 2^{2\alpha j_1} ) = O( T + T^{ \frac{2\alpha}{\alpha+1} } ) = O( T )∣∣f−fM​∣∣2⩽∣∣f−f~​M​∣∣2=O(2j2​+22αj1​)=O(T+Tα+12α​)=O(T)

and the number of coefficients as

M=O(T−1+T−2/(α+1))=O(T−1).M=O(T^{-1}+T^{-2/(\alpha+1)}) = O(T^{-1} ).M=O(T−1+T−2/(α+1))=O(T−1).

Since α⩾1\alpha\geqslant 1α⩾1, choose TTT of order M−1M^{-1}M−1 with a sufficiently large constant. This meets the coefficient budget and gives the asserted error. For 0<α<10<\alpha<10<α<1, the same argument gives O(M−α)O(M^{-\alpha})O(M−α) instead.

The wavelet rate improves on the O(M−1/2)O(M^{-1/2})O(M−1/2) Fourier rate (5.20), but it still fails to exploit the full Cα\text{C}^\alphaCα regularity away from the edge curves.

This rate also holds for the broader bounded-variation model (5.11), for which wavelet approximation is asymptotically optimal.

Figure 5.18. 2-D wavelet approximation.

Figure 5.18 shows wavelet approximations of a bounded variation image.

5.6 Approximation of Cartoon Images¶

The isotropic, compactly supported wavelets considered here occupy squares that do not follow the smooth contours of geometric images (5.13). These contours have more structure than the finite-length level sets allowed by the bounded-variation model (5.11).

5.6.1 Wavelet Approximation of Cartoon Images¶

The bound (5.31) gives a wavelet approximation rate of O(M−1)O(M^{-1})O(M−1) for cartoon images (5.13). Even the simple indicator f=1Ωf=1_\Omegaf=1Ω​, where Ω\OmegaΩ is a disk, can attain this slow rate: isotropic wavelets do not efficiently follow its curved boundary. The smoothed cartoon model (5.14) can behave similarly when the coefficient budget MMM is too small to resolve the blur.

Figure 5.19 shows that many large coefficients are located near edge curves, and retaining only a small number leads to a poor approximation with visually unpleasant artifacts.

Figure 5.19. Wavelet approximation of a cartoon image.

5.6.2 Finite Element Approximation¶

An adaptive triangulation can improve the approximation by using elongated triangles aligned with the edges. Figure 5.20 shows an example of such a triangulation.

Figure 5.20. A cartoon with smooth variation on both sides of an elliptical jump, a triangulation elongated along that boundary, and the continuous P1P_1P1​ interpolant.

Select MMM points in the image domain [0,1]2[0,1]^2[0,1]2 and connect them into a triangulation. Define f~M\tilde f_Mf~​M​ by piecewise affine interpolation on the resulting triangles.

Figure 5.21. The same mesh over a lightened P1P_1P1​ interpolant (left), with the boxed boundary region enlarged (right). Thin triangles follow the red singularity curve; the arrow indicates its tangent. Smooth regions use nearly equilateral elements.

Figure 5.21 illustrates a construction for C2\text{C}^{2}C2 cartoon images (5.13) with α=2\alpha=2α=2. In smooth regions, use ≈M/2\approx M/2≈M/2 nearly equilateral triangles of width ≈M−1/2\approx M^{-1/2}≈M−1/2. Near the edges, exploit the C2\text{C}^{2}C2 contour regularity by placing ≈M/2\approx M/2≈M/2 elongated triangles of length ≈M−1\approx M^{-1}≈M−1 along the contours and width ≈M−2\approx M^{-2}≈M−2 across them. Such a triangulation yields the error bound

∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣2=O(M−2),(5.32)|\!| f-f_M |\!|^2 = O(M^{-2}), \tag{5.32}∣∣f−fM​∣∣2=O(M−2),(5.32)

which improves over the wavelet approximation error decay (5.31).

Implementing this construction requires estimating the edges. This is particularly difficult for blurred cartoon images with an unknown smoothing kernel hhh.

Practical methods use heuristics or greedy rules to select sample points and triangulate them from discrete or noisy data. Figure 5.22 uses a known synthetic contour to isolate the effect of mesh geometry. Both regions have smooth, nonaffine intensities. The displayed P1P_1P1​ image is decoded from an explicit mesh stream whose bit count includes vertex coordinates, values, connectivity, and headers; this example does not assume an optimal mesh code.

Figure 5.22. Compression of a piecewise-smooth cartoon using a contour-aligned mesh and JPEG-2000 at the same transmitted bit budget. From left to right: original, mesh, decoded P1P_1P1​ image, and JPEG-2000 image. Mesh costs include coordinates, nodal values, connectivity, and headers.

5.6.3 Curvelet Approximation¶

A fixed family of oriented, anisotropic atoms offers an alternative to adaptive triangulations. Candès and Donoho introduced the curvelet frame for this purpose [5].

Curvelets.

At fine scales j⩽0j\leqslant 0j⩽0, the geometry can be illustrated by applying parabolic scaling to a horizontally oriented mother function ccc,

c2j(x1,x2)≈2−3j/4c(2−j/2x1,2−jx2),c_{2^j}(x_1,x_2) \approx 2^{-3j/4} c(2^{-j/2} x_1, 2^{-j} x_2),c2j​(x1​,x2​)≈2−3j/4c(2−j/2x1​,2−jx2​),

followed by translation and rotation,

c2j,uθ(x1,x2)=c2j(R−θ(x−u))c_{2^j,u}^\theta(x_1,x_2) = c_{2^j}(R_{-\theta}(x-u))c2j,uθ​(x1​,x2​)=c2j​(R−θ​(x−u))

where RθR_\thetaRθ​ is the rotation of angle θ\thetaθ.

The atom c2j,uθc_{2^j,u}^\thetac2j,uθ​ is localized near uuu and oriented at angle θ\thetaθ. Its dimensions obey “width ≈\approx≈ length2^22”, the same relation used for adaptive triangles near edges. This scaling matches the contour geometry of the cartoon model (5.13) with α=2\alpha=2α=2.

Figure 5.23. A curvelet cmc_mcm​ in space (left) and its localization in the Fourier domain (right).

Figure 5.23 illustrates this localization in space and frequency.

Parameter discretization.

To build an image representation, one needs to sample the position uuu and orientation θ\thetaθ. The angular sampling interval depends on the scale:

∀ 0⩽k<2−⌈j/2⌉+2,θk(j)=kπ2⌈j/2⌉−1\forall \,0 \leqslant k < 2^{-\lceil j/2 \rceil+2}, \quad \theta_{k}^{(j)} = k \pi 2^{ \lceil j/2 \rceil -1 }∀0⩽k<2−⌈j/2⌉+2,θk(j)​=kπ2⌈j/2⌉−1

and the spatial grid depends on both scale and orientation:

∀ m=(m1,m2)∈Z2,um(j,θ)=Rθ(2j/2m1,2jm2).\forall \,m=(m_1,m_2) \in \mathbb{Z}^2, \quad u_m^{(j,\theta)} = R_\theta( 2^{j/2} m_1, 2^j m_2 ).∀m=(m1​,m2​)∈Z2,um(j,θ)​=Rθ​(2j/2m1​,2jm2​).

Figure 5.24 shows this sampling pattern.

Figure 5.24. Sampling pattern for the curvelet positions.

Curvelet tight frame.

The scaling and sampling formulas above describe the geometry of curvelets. An exact tight frame additionally requires carefully chosen frequency windows and a low-frequency family; an arbitrary mother function ccc does not suffice. With this construction, write the complete family as (Cλ)λ∈Λ(C_\lambda)_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(Cλ​)λ∈Λ​, where Λ\LambdaΛ includes the fine-scale indices (j,m,k)(j,m,k)(j,m,k) and the low-frequency indices. Then

∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣2=∑λ∈Λ∣⟨f, Cλ⟩∣2,f=∑λ∈Λ⟨f, Cλ⟩Cλ.|\!| f |\!|^2=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}|\langle f,\,C_\lambda\rangle|^2, \qquad f=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\langle f,\,C_\lambda\rangle C_\lambda.∣∣f∣∣2=λ∈Λ∑​∣⟨f,Cλ​⟩∣2,f=λ∈Λ∑​⟨f,Cλ​⟩Cλ​.

The reconstruction converges in L2L^2L2. These are the Parseval-frame identities; the family is redundant and its atoms are not mutually orthogonal.

One discrete construction for an image with NNN pixels uses ≈5N\approx 5 N≈5N atoms [7].

Curvelet approximation.

A nonlinear MMM-term approximation in curvelets is defined as

fM=∑λ∈Λ: ∣⟨f, Cλ⟩∣>T⟨f, Cλ⟩Cλf_M = \sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda:\,|\langle f,\,C_\lambda\rangle| > T} \langle f,\,C_\lambda\rangle C_\lambdafM​=λ∈Λ:∣⟨f,Cλ​⟩∣>T∑​⟨f,Cλ​⟩Cλ​

The complete index set Λ\LambdaΛ includes the low-frequency family, and the threshold TTT determines the number MMM of retained coefficients. As before, ties require a selection rule if an exact coefficient count is prescribed. Because the frame is not orthogonal, fMf_MfM​ need not be the best MMM-term curvelet approximation.

Far from an edge, at locations um(j,θ)u_m^{(j,\theta)}um(j,θ)​, cancellation makes the coefficients ⟨f, Cj,m,k⟩\langle f,\,C_{j,m,k}\rangle⟨f,Cj,m,k​⟩ small. When um(j,θ)u_m^{(j,\theta)}um(j,θ)​ lies near an edge with tangent direction θ~\tilde\thetaθ~, the coefficient ⟨f, Cj,m,k⟩\langle f,\,C_{j,m,k}\rangle⟨f,Cj,m,k​⟩ rapidly decreases as the orientation mismatch ∣θ−θ~∣|\theta-\tilde \theta|∣θ−θ~∣ grows. Figure 5.25 compares this adaptation to edges with the square supports of directional wavelets.

Figure 5.25. Wavelet (left) and curvelet (right) approximation of a cartoon image.

Combining spatial cancellation, directional selectivity, and scale-dependent sampling gives the approximation bound

∣ ⁣∣f−fM∣ ⁣∣2=O(log⁡3(M)M−2)|\!| f-f_M |\!|^2 = O(\log^3(M) M^{-2})∣∣f−fM​∣∣2=O(log3(M)M−2)

for images in the cartoon model (5.13) for α=2\alpha=2α=2. This nearly matches the adaptive-triangulation rate (5.32), while allowing fMf_MfM​ to be computed in O(Nlog⁡(N))O(N \log(N))O(Nlog(N)) operations for an image of NNN pixels.

Redundancy complicates the use of curvelets for compression, but their approximation properties are useful for denoising geometric images and textures. Figure 5.26 compares curvelet and wavelet denoising using the thresholding method of Section 7.3.1.

Figure 5.26. Comparison of translation-invariant wavelet denoising and curvelet denoising.
